books.section: Topic 7.7 1920s: Innovations in Communication and Technology

stimulus.text: Paraphrase of Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 9, Topic 7.7: In 1927, record producer Ralph Peer traveled through the South to record local string bands, balladeers, and other musicians in gospel, blues, and ragtime. Sessions held in Bristol, Tennessee, launched nationally known country performers Jimmie Rodgers and the Carter Family. Record companies had begun issuing “hillbilly” records in 1923 and 1924.
stimulus.source_note: Paraphrase of Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 9, Topic 7.7.

stem: Radio and recording in the 1920s are best compared as technologies that both

options.text: served only listeners living in big cities
options.misconception: Radio and records reached farms and small towns, not only big cities. Rural listeners were a large part of the audience.

options.text: were owned by the federal government itself
options.misconception: Neither was government-owned. Private networks and record companies ran them.

rationales.A: Radio and records reached farms and small towns, not only big cities. Rural listeners were a large part of the audience.
rationales.B: Neither was government-owned. Private networks and record companies ran them.
rationales.C: Books and newspapers kept going. Radio and records added new media; they did not replace print.
rationales.D: Radio carried the same programs everywhere, while records carried local sounds like the Bristol sessions outward. Both mixed local roots into one shared culture.
rationales.general:
1. Take radio first: one program reached listeners in every region at once.
2. Take recording next: local sounds from Bristol reached listeners far away.
3. Combine them: both mixed local roots into one culture that Americans shared.
4. Note the balance: the shared culture kept local sounds alive instead of wiping them out.
Remember: a mass medium can spread one program and many local sounds at the same time.
